title: a married surname is a woman's
line: a surname a record writes is read as a married one only for a woman: the obituary names Charles Miller, a son-in-law, and a card an older matcher left puts him to his brother-in-law Charles Beckam Davidson, whom the rule created from the same notice; Miller is the surname of a son-in-law on the record, but the record and the tree both say he is a man, so the surname disagrees, the card says so, and the rule refuses him on the name

steps.say: Robert Edgar Davidson's obituary, naming his brothers and sisters, his daughter Carol Miller and her husband Charles Miller
its subject accepted by the owner: the rule creates the brothers and sisters it names, Charles Beckam Davidson among them
a card an older matcher left, putting the son-in-law Charles Miller to Charles Beckam Davidson

disagree.some: surname disagrees (record Charles Miller, tree Charles Beckam Davidson)

expect.why: the son-in-law's own surname beside himself makes no married name of it: he is a man on the record and in the tree
